title: Draft Discovery Plan Memorandum for Breach of Contract and Fraud Defense

blind.coverage: I read all 65 criteria and the instructions. I read these documents in full: the case management order, the Hartwell litigation hold memo, the Ostrowski email chain, Pinnacle's hold notice, the pre-litigation correspondence (April 5 demand and April 22 Liu response), and the relevant sections of the Aldersgate assessment (executive summary, hold review, custodians, the Brecker phone, binders, QualTrack, volume and cost). For the MSA, complaint, answer/counterclaim and Whitmore report I did not read everything; I searched them for the facts the criteria rely on (the Section 12 limitation text, Sections 4.3–4.4, 8.1–8.2, 14.3–14.4, 15.1, the damages figures, torque/installation, the 19 UT valves, the foundry heat-treatment finding, Rule 9(b), and joint-inspection attendees). A CourtListener semantic search on Ohio fraud/limitation-of-liability law returned nothing on point. So I did not independently verify the Ohio proposition in C-014, and I did not flag it; it is a widely accepted principle. No primary case text was read in this session, so every authority is marked unverified. I read the judge prompt and the solver system prompt; the judge sees the criterion title as well as match_criteria.

findings.title: Hold-delay criteria treat the Sept 25, 2024 notice as the trigger; the record puts the preservation duty in April 2024
findings.explanation: C-001 (title '35-day delay') and C-002/C-003 measure the preservation gap from Pinnacle's Sept 25, 2024 hold notice or the Sept 23 Complaint. But Pinnacle's April 5, 2024 demand letter threatened suit and expressly demanded preservation, text messages included. Liu received it April 8 and wrote on April 22 that Hartwell 'will take appropriate steps to preserve documents.' The CMO states the duty arose 'at the latest, when litigation was reasonably anticipated.' The real gap is about 6.5 months, which is far worse for Hartwell and widens the loss window C-003 asks counsel to check. A competent memo built on the correct April 2024 trigger may not frame the problem as a '35-day delay', and a strict judge could fail it on C-001. Meanwhile a memo that understates the exposure by using the Sept 25 trigger passes. Aldersgate uses the same 35-day framing, which is probably where the rubric got it, but the primary documents contradict it.

evidence.quote: Pinnacle hereby demands that Hartwell immediately take all steps necessary to identify, locate, and preserve all documents... including but not limited to emails, text messages
Hartwell will take appropriate steps to preserve documents and materials relevant to the matters raised in your correspondence.
Hartwell's duty to preserve arose no later than the filing of that Complaint and arguably earlier — upon receipt of Pinnacle's formal demand letter dated April 5, 2024
This obligation arose, at the latest, when litigation was reasonably anticipated
approximately 35 days after receiving Pinnacle's litigation hold notice on September 25, 2024

authorities.citation: Fed. R. Civ. P. 37(e) & 2015 Advisory Committee Note
authorities.proposition: The duty to preserve ESI attaches when litigation is reasonably anticipated, not only when suit is filed or a hold notice arrives.

findings.suggested_fix: Reframe C-001 to pass a memo that flags the late Oct 30, 2024 hold measured against the April 2024 demand and/or the Sept 2024 notice and Complaint. Accept either framing in C-002/C-003, and ideally credit identifying the April 2024 trigger.

findings.title: Rubric calls §12.2 a 'consequential damages cap'; the MSA bars consequential damages outright and caps all liability
findings.explanation: C-013 and C-050 require stating that the MSA's 'consequential damages cap' is $5,811,300. In the MSA, §12.1 excludes consequential damages (lost revenue, business interruption) entirely, carving out gross negligence and willful misconduct. Separately, §12.2 caps aggregate liability on all claims, expressly including 'misrepresentation', at 150% of Total Contract Price. The 'consequential damages cap' label comes from both pleadings, which misdescribe the contract. The difference is material: under the actual text, the $8.42M downtime claim is barred outright unless willful misconduct is shown, and the fraud argument runs through the §12.1 carve-out and the §12.2 'misrepresentation' language. A memo that reads the MSA correctly risks failing C-050 ('stated incorrectly'), while a memo copying the pleadings' error passes.

evidence.quote: IN NO EVENT SHALL EITHER PARTY BE LIABLE TO THE OTHER PARTY FOR ANY INDIRECT, INCIDENTAL, SPECIAL, CONSEQUENTIAL... PROVIDED, HOWEVER, THAT THIS EXCLUSION SHALL NOT APPLY TO: (A) DAMAGES ARISING FROM A PARTY'S GROSS NEGLIGENCE OR WILLFUL MISCONDUCT

THE AGGREGATE LIABILITY OF EITHER PARTY TO THE OTHER PARTY FOR ALL CLAIMS... SHALL NOT EXCEED ONE HUNDRED FIFTY PERCENT (150%) OF THE TOTAL CONTRACT PRICE... INCLUDING WITHOUT LIMITATION... MISREPRESENTATION
Section 12 of the MSA expressly limits consequential damages recoverable by either party to one hundred fifty percent (150%) of the total contract price
PASS if the memo states that the MSA's consequential damages cap is $5,811,300 (150% of $3,874,200).

findings.suggested_fix: Rewrite C-013/C-050 to refer to the §12.2 aggregate liability cap of $5,811,300 and accept either characterization, or credit a memo that distinguishes the §12.1 exclusion (with its willful-misconduct carve-out) from the §12.2 cap.

findings.title: C-031 says the hold 'focused on electronic records', but the hold expressly covers paper files and binders
findings.explanation: C-031 adopts Aldersgate's description that the Oct 30 hold covered only electronic records and did not include the binders. The hold itself forbids discarding 'paper files, binders, notebooks, or other physical materials' and tells custodians to 'identify and segregate' physical files, and Kowalski, who keeps the binders, is a named recipient. The real gap is narrower: there is no specific directive naming the QA lot binders or QA staff beyond the custodians. A memo that reads the hold accurately and concludes the binders are generically covered, while recommending an inventory, could fail C-031. Most memos will still call out the absence of a specific binder directive, so this is arguable rather than certain misgrading. The underlying Aldersgate inaccuracy is itself a document defect.

evidence.quote: Dispose of, recycle, or discard any paper files, binders, notebooks, or other physical materials related to the above subject matters.
These hardcopy binders are not referenced in Hartwell's October 30, 2024 litigation hold notice, which focused exclusively on electronic records.
were not specifically included in Hartwell's October 30, 2024 litigation hold (which focused on electronic records)

findings.suggested_fix: Drop the 'focused on electronic records' premise. Pass any memo that flags the lack of a specific preservation directive or inventory for the HV-4400 QA binders, including one that notes the hold's generic paper-records language.

findings.title: C-025 offers a Rule 9(b) particularity challenge as an early partial summary judgment ground
findings.explanation: C-025 gives 'early partial summary judgment... on the fraud claim (Rule 9(b) particularity)' as an example of linking phasing to dispositive motions. Rule 9(b) is a pleading standard. It is tested on the pleadings (here Rule 12(c), since Hartwell has answered) and needs no discovery phase. The usual remedy is leave to amend: the amendment deadline is April 30, 2025, and the Ostrowski emails, which must be produced, supply the missing particulars. So the criterion rewards a legally confused strategy. It also says the memo must be 'noting' the Jan 15, 2026 and Oct 31, 2025 dates, while the FAIL condition only requires a link to dispositive-motion strategy, leaving unclear whether the dates are mandatory. Because the damages-cap alternative is valid and C-043's FAIL bar is low, the misgrade risk is moderate.

evidence.quote: such as on the fraud claim (Rule 9(b) particularity) or on the consequential damages cap, noting that the dispositive motions deadline is January 15, 2026 and the discovery cutoff is October 31, 2025
Any motion to amend the pleadings or to join additional parties shall be filed no later than April 30, 2025.
Pinnacle is confident that targeted discovery into Hartwell's internal quality records, communications, and decision-making processes will confirm and substantiate the allegations

authorities.proposition: Particularity is a pleading requirement tested on the pleadings, with leave to amend freely given; summary judgment tests evidentiary sufficiency.

findings.suggested_fix: Remove 9(b) as an example of a summary judgment ground (or say 'Rule 12(c) motion'), keep the cap-enforceability example, and state plainly whether citing the specific deadlines is required.

findings.title: Three criteria rest on a joint-inspection privilege issue the record barely supports; C-028 also misstates waiver law
findings.explanation: The complaint, answer and Whitmore report list the May 10, 2024 inspection attendees without Liu. Only Aldersgate says she 'attended or coordinated' it. The record contains no attorney communications shared at the inspection. C-028 credits the 'risk of privilege waiver when attorney communications... are shared with non-attorney personnel.' Sharing within the client company (Liu to Kowalski) does not waive privilege under Upjohn; waiver comes from disclosure to the adversary. Common interest between adversaries is not a live question. C-029 then requires specifically treating Liu's 'consulted with our quality assurance team' line as a privilege or subject-matter-waiver concern. A competent memo might instead treat that letter as a credibility or Liu-as-fact-witness problem, given Kowalski's knowledge of the Ostrowski emails. Under all-pass grading, three stacked criteria on one speculative issue sharply raise the chance of failing sound work.

evidence.quote: the inspection was attended by Diane Kowalski (Hartwell's Director of Quality), Sandra Reeves (Pinnacle's Vice President of Engineering), and Dr. Franklin Cho
attended or coordinated the joint inspection on May 10, 2024. NOTE: Privilege review will be critical for this custodian's documents
the risk of privilege waiver when attorney communications or strategy discussions are shared with non-attorney personnel in the context of joint activities with the opposing party
Upon receipt of your demand letter, I consulted with our quality assurance team, including our Director of Quality

authorities.citation: Upjohn Co. v. United States, 449 U.S. 383 (1981)
authorities.proposition: Communications between corporate counsel and non-management employees made to obtain legal advice are privileged; sharing within the corporation does not itself waive privilege.
Subject-matter waiver extends only to intentional disclosures where fairness requires undisclosed material to be considered together with disclosed material.

findings.suggested_fix: Merge C-027–C-029 into one criterion that passes any memo addressing privilege review or logging of Liu's pre-litigation and joint-inspection communications, or the waiver or at-issue risk from her April 22 letter. Remove the intra-company-sharing waiver premise from C-028.

blind.overall: The rubric is mostly well grounded. Most of its 65 criteria track specific, verifiable facts in the record: the hold gaps (Ostrowski, texts, QualTrack), the Brecker phone, the Ostrowski email chain, the Great Lakes and Whitmore findings, the damages arithmetic, and the CMO dates and ESI topics. Many are demanding but implicit in a Rule 26(f) discovery plan memo, especially since the CMO itself lists custodian prioritization, format, search methodology, phasing and proportionality. The main defects are substantive. The hold-delay criteria measure spoliation exposure from the Sept 2024 notice even though the April 2024 demand letter, and Liu's promise to preserve, triggered the duty. The cap criteria repeat the pleadings' mischaracterization of MSA §12 as a 'consequential damages cap' when §12.1 excludes consequential damages and §12.2 caps aggregate liability. Smaller problems: a Rule 9(b)/summary-judgment conflation in C-025, three stacked privilege criteria built on a thin joint-inspection record, and a binder criterion that repeats Aldersgate's inaccurate description of the hold. Under all-pass grading, the O1 and O2 issues alone could fail a legally sharper memo, so those criteria should be revised before the task is used for headline scoring.

sol_verdicts.reason: The hold memo goes to Kowalski. It forbids discarding 'paper files, binders, notebooks, or other physical materials' and directs custodians to segregate physical files. Aldersgate's statements that the hold 'focused exclusively on electronic records' and 'does not specifically reference hardcopy' contradict the hold's own text. C-031 adopts that false premise and asks the memo to assert a gap. A memo that reads the hold accurately (binders are generically covered, so inventory and confirm them) could be failed.

C-025 names Rule 9(b) particularity as a summary judgment ground. That is a pleading-standard issue tested under Rule 12(c), not Rule 56, and it is unclear whether citing the dates is mandatory. The cap alternative is valid, so this is arguable. C-043 only requires discussing Hartwell's 9(b) defense tied to phasing or dispositive strategy. The Answer pleads that defense and CMO §VII names 9(b) sufficiency as an early issue, so C-043 is grounded and not a defect.

Under Upjohn, sharing privileged communications within the company (Liu to Kowalski) does not waive privilege. Waiver comes from disclosure to the adversary. The record also shows no attorney communications shared at the inspection. Liu's statement that she 'consulted with our quality assurance team' reveals no privileged substance. A competent memo might treat that line as a credibility or fact-witness issue rather than subject-matter waiver and still fail C-029. Some memos will address these points anyway, so arguable.

CMO §VII encourages parties to discuss phasing but does not require it. With the Ostrowski emails undercutting any early fraud motion, a defense lawyer could reasonably consider phasing and decline it, and C-023/C-024 would fail that memo. So arguable. C-036 is implicit: CMO ESI topic 8 is 'Custodian identification and prioritization', Aldersgate supplies tiers, and the criterion accepts any 'similar prioritization'.

The PASS standard is lenient. It accepts a memo that 'otherwise explains the legal principle that fraud can void contractual damages caps' and fails only a memo that assumes the cap definitively applies. The principle that a party cannot contract away liability for its own intentional fraud is widely accepted, and the complaint pleads it. A competent memo would at least flag it, even while noting that §12.2 expressly lists 'misrepresentation'. My CourtListener search returned nothing on point, so this is unverified but low-risk.

findings.title: C-031 premises a binder preservation gap on a hold 'focused on electronic records'; the hold expressly covers binders
findings.explanation: C-031 repeats Aldersgate's description of the Oct 30 hold as electronic-only and asks the memo to identify that the binders were not included, creating a gap. The hold itself, which went to Kowalski, forbids discarding 'paper files, binders, notebooks, or other physical materials' and directs custodians to segregate physical files. Aldersgate's report misdescribes the hold, which is a document defect. The real gap is narrower: no directive names the lot binders, and QA staff beyond the named custodians were not instructed. A memo that reads the hold correctly and says the binders are covered but should be inventoried and confirmed could fail. A memo that repeats Aldersgate's error passes.

evidence.quote: Dispose of, recycle, or discard any paper files, binders, notebooks, or other physical materials related to the above subject matters.
not referenced in Hartwell's October 30, 2024 litigation hold notice, which focused exclusively on electronic records
were not specifically included in Hartwell's October 30, 2024 litigation hold (which focused on electronic records)

findings.suggested_fix: Drop the 'focused on electronic records' premise. Pass any memo that flags the binders for specific preservation, inventory or confirmation, including one that notes the hold's generic coverage of paper records.

findings.title: Hold-delay criteria measure the gap from the Sept 2024 notice; the April 2024 demand letter likely triggered the duty
findings.explanation: Pinnacle's April 5, 2024 demand threatened suit and expressly demanded preservation, including text messages. Liu promised on April 22 to preserve. Under the CMO, the duty arose 'at the latest, when litigation was reasonably anticipated'. The rubric frames the problem as a '35-day delay' from the Sept 25 notice. That framing understates Hartwell's roughly 6.5-month exposure and narrows the loss window for remediation. findings.suggested_fix: Pass a memo that flags the late Oct 30 hold measured from either the April 2024 demand or the Sept 2024 notice and Complaint, and credit identifying the April trigger.

findings.title: Rubric calls the $5,811,300 figure a 'consequential damages cap'; MSA §12.1 excludes consequential damages and §12.2 caps aggregate liability
findings.explanation: Both pleadings mislabel §12. Under §12.1, consequential damages (lost revenue, business interruption) are excluded outright, with a carve-out for gross negligence and willful misconduct. Under §12.2, aggregate liability on all claims, expressly including misrepresentation, is capped at 150% of Total Contract Price. C-013 and C-050 adopt the pleadings' label. Downgraded from problematic: the amount is correct, and most judges would pass a memo that states $5,811,300 under the correct label. A strict reading of 'stated incorrectly' could still penalize a memo that corrects the label, and the rubric rewards a mischaracterization that matters to the analysis (the $8.42M downtime claim is barred by §12.1 rather than capped).

evidence.quote: 12.2 Cap on Liability. NOTWITHSTANDING ANYTHING TO THE CONTRARY IN THIS AGREEMENT, THE AGGREGATE LIABILITY OF EITHER PARTY
the consequential damages cap under Section 12 is $5,811,300
PASS if the memo states that the MSA's consequential damages cap is $5,811,300

findings.suggested_fix: Refer to the '§12 liability cap ($5,811,300)' and accept any accurate characterization, including one that distinguishes the §12.1 exclusion from the §12.2 cap.

findings.title: C-025 offers Rule 9(b) particularity as an early partial summary judgment ground; deadline 'noting' requirement unclear
findings.explanation: Rule 9(b) is a pleading standard. Once Hartwell has answered, it is tested by a Rule 12(c) motion, and amendment is usually allowed (the amendment deadline is April 30, 2025, and the Ostrowski emails supply particulars). It is not tested by Rule 56. It is offered only as an example beside a valid cap-enforceability example, so the misgrade risk is moderate. The PASS text says 'noting' the Jan 15, 2026 and Oct 31, 2025 dates, but the FAIL condition does not require them, which creates ambiguity. C-043 is dropped: it is grounded in the Answer and CMO §VII.

evidence.quote: such as on the fraud claim (Rule 9(b) particularity) or on the consequential damages cap, noting that the dispositive motions deadline is January 15, 2026
the sufficiency of fraud allegations under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 9(b)

authorities.proposition: Particularity is tested on the pleadings; summary judgment tests evidentiary sufficiency.

findings.suggested_fix: Replace the example with 'Rule 12(c) or early motion on fraud-claim sufficiency', keep the cap example, and state whether the dates are required.

findings.title: C-028/C-029 treat intra-company sharing and Liu's 'consulted with QA' line as waiver risks
findings.explanation: Under Upjohn, sharing privileged communications within the company (Liu to Kowalski) does not waive privilege. Waiver follows from disclosure to the adversary, and the record contains no attorney communications shared at the May 10 inspection. Liu's letter reveals the fact of the consultation, not its substance. Subject-matter waiver under FRE 502(a) requires an intentional disclosure of privileged content. C-029 requires treating that line specifically as a privilege concern, so a memo that treats it as a credibility or Liu-as-witness issue fails. C-027 is dropped: Aldersgate grounds a general privilege-review concern for Liu tied to the inspection.

evidence.quote: the risk of privilege waiver when attorney communications or strategy discussions are shared with non-attorney personnel
Upon receipt of your demand letter, I consulted with our quality assurance team, including our Director of Quality

authorities.citation: Upjohn Co. v. United States, 449 U.S. 383 (1981)
authorities.proposition: Counsel's communications with employees to obtain legal advice are privileged.
Subject-matter waiver requires an intentional disclosure where fairness requires it.

findings.suggested_fix: Merge the two criteria into one that passes any reasoned privilege analysis of Liu's pre-litigation and inspection communications, including a reasoned no-waiver conclusion.

findings.title: Phasing is mandated, although the CMO only invites discussion and declining it is defensible
findings.explanation: CMO §VII encourages the parties to discuss phasing and makes it optional ('If the parties agree'). For Hartwell, an early fraud-viability phase would front-load production of the damaging Ostrowski emails, so a competent defense memo could weigh phasing and recommend an integrated schedule. C-023 and C-024 would fail that memo. Most memos will propose phasing, so this is arguable. C-036 (custodian prioritization) is implicit under CMO ESI topic 8 and is not flagged.

evidence.quote: The Court encourages the parties to discuss at the Rule 26(f) conference whether discovery should be conducted in phases.
FAIL if discovery is not proposed in phases

findings.suggested_fix: Pass a memo that either proposes phasing with a rationale or analyzes phasing and gives reasons for declining it.

final.changes_from_blind: I adopted one finding from Sol's F4: C-023 and C-024 mandate phasing, although the CMO only invites discussion of it. I rejected C-036 as a defect because CMO ESI topic 8 makes custodian prioritization implicit. I raised the binder finding (C-031) from arguable to problematic after rechecking the documents: the hold memo goes to Kowalski and expressly covers binders, so the criterion's parenthetical premise is factually wrong, and Sol independently reached the same conclusion. I downgraded the hold-delay finding (C-001–C-003) from problematic to arguable. The 35-day gap is factually accurate and most memos will cite both dates; the April trigger point is about understated exposure, not a certain misgrade. I downgraded the cap-label finding (C-013/C-050) to arguable because the amount is correct and judges will likely pass a memo that uses the correct label. I removed C-014 from the cap finding, since its lenient standard is sound. I dropped C-043 from the 9(b) finding (the Answer pleads the defense and CMO §VII names 9(b)) and C-027 from the privilege finding (Aldersgate grounds it). I rejected Sol's F5 on C-014 as not a defect.
final.coverage: I reviewed all 65 criteria in the blind pass and re-read the criteria relevant to Sol's findings and my own. In this pass I rechecked the hold memo (recipients and physical-materials language), Aldersgate's binder and custodian-tier sections, CMO §§ on phasing, preservation and ESI topics, MSA §12, and the complaint's cap and fraud allegations.
